statement: In people who inject drugs attending two rural syringe services programmes in North Carolina and West Virginia (recruited June 2021 to March 2022), recent use of fentanyl test strips was less common a year after the start than at the start, and not clearly different after six months: the adjusted odds of having used strips in the past 30 days were 0.642 times those at the start at 12 months (95% CI 0.447 to 0.923; all 541 people) and 0.557 times (0.364 to 0.853) in the 212 who answered all three surveys, and 0.936 times (0.696 to 1.258) at 6 months, while the share of those 212 who had ever used strips rose from 65 to 80 in 100. The share using strips at each survey is not printed, so the size of the fall cannot be given as a number out of 100. 213 of the 541 gave no follow-up and had used strips less often, which could bias the trend, and why use fell was not measured (the authors suggest that a test for fentanyl alone tells people less once fentanyl is expected). Over a few weeks, young adults in a Rhode Island pilot used a median of 3 of the 10 strips they were given (10 of 81 used all ten); in that pilot and in a British Columbia take-home programme, 95 or 96 in 100 said they would use strips again, an intention rather than a measure of use. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In the one study that followed people for a year (people who inject drugs at two rural US programmes), fewer had used test strips recently after 12 months than at the start, though more had used them at some point. The study lost many people along the way and did not measure why use fell. In shorter studies almost everyone said they would use strips again, but that is a plan, not a measure.
population: People who inject drugs (aged 18 or over) recruited at two rural syringe services programmes in North Carolina and West Virginia, June 2021 to March 2022, surveyed at baseline, 6 and 12 months (541 at baseline; 212 at all three); for short-term use, young adults in a Rhode Island pilot (2017) and people returning take-home kits in British Columbia (2019)
outcome: Self-reported fentanyl test strip use in the past 30 days (and ever); in the short term, the number of strips used and the stated wish to use strips again
magnitude: Past-30-day use, adjusted odds ratios against baseline (mixed-effects logistic regression): 12 months 0.642 (0.447–0.923; 541 people, 1081 observations) and 0.557 (0.364–0.853; 212 complete cases, 636 observations); 6 months 0.936 (0.696–1.258) and 0.946 (0.650–1.375). Lifetime use among complete cases 65.1% at baseline, 77.8% at 6 months and 79.7% at 12 months. No follow-up: 213 of 541 (39.4%, editors' calculation), who had less often used strips (54.3% against 65.1%). Krieger: median 3 strips (IQR 1–6) within a few weeks; 10 of 81 used all ten; 77/81 (95%) would like to use strips in future. Klaire: 322/336 answers (95.8%) would use strips again.

evidence.locator: Abstract › Methods; Methods, 1st paragraph; Results › Descriptive findings, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: People who inject drugs (aged 18 or over, injected in the past 30 days) were recruited at two syringe services programmes in rural North Carolina and West Virginia and surveyed at baseline, 6 and 12 months; of 541 who completed baseline, 328 completed at least one follow-up and 212 both.

evidence.locator: Abstract › Results; Table 1 (p. 2); Results › Model results, 1st paragraph (p. 3)
evidence.extracted: Adjusted odds of past-30-day strip use against baseline (mixed-effects logistic regression): at 12 months 0.642 (95% CI 0.447–0.923) in the full sample (541 people, 1081 observations) and 0.557 (0.364–0.853) in complete cases (212 people, 636 observations); at 6 months 0.936 (0.696–1.258) and 0.946 (0.650–1.375). The share using strips at each survey is not given in the main text.
Among complete cases, lifetime strip use rose from 65.1% at baseline to 77.8% at 6 months and 79.7% at 12 months.

Compared with the complete-case sample, the 213 participants with no follow-up had less often witnessed an overdose (56.8% against 69.8%) and less often used strips (54.3% against 65.1%). The authors read the decline as testing for fentanyl telling people less once fentanyl is expected, not as unwillingness to check drugs; reasons for testing, strip supply and contact with services were not measured. Editors' calculation: 213 of 541 is 39.4%.

Over the first few weeks, participants used a median of 3 of their 10 strips (IQR 1–6) and 10 used all ten; 77 of 81 (95%) said they would like to use strips in future, more often among those who had used a strip (61 of 62 against 16 of 19, p = 0.041).
322 of 336 survey answers (95.8%) said they would use the strips again; 323 (96.1%) found the instructions easy to follow and 319 (94.9%) felt confident reading the results.

evidence.locator: Results › Feasibility of FTS Use › Overall satisfaction with use; Feasibility of FTS distribution as a public health intervention, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: As relayed: 49% to 96% of participants across studies found strips useful and wanted to use them again (per-study values in a supplement not read); few distribution studies report a net change in strip use, either in the number of people using strips or in how often they use them.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E high: 39 in 100 had no follow-up and those lost had used strips less; use was self-reported; strip supply and contact with services were not measured.

indirectness.note: Two rural programmes in two US states with a fentanyl-dominated supply, people who inject drugs only; the short-term figures are a paid pilot and stated intentions.

imprecision.note: The 12-month intervals exclude no change; the size of the fall in absolute terms cannot be given because the shares at each survey are not printed.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim (a trend over time); observational, starts low; risk of bias and indirectness each take a level: very low. Status single study: one cohort measured use over a year; the stated wish to use strips again (Rhode Island, British Columbia) is an intention, not continued use.
